sentences.text: The genus is known exclusively from its teeth, which are laterally compressed, curved, and serrated.
The holotype jaws measure 193 millimeters in length and bear teeth with a distinctive serration density of five to six denticles per millimeter.
The holotype jaws of Richardoestesia were discovered in 1917 by Charles Hazelius Sternberg and his sons in Alberta, Canada.
The genus Richardoestesia was formally named in 1990 by Phillip Currie, John Keith Rigby, and Robert Evan Sloan.
Teeth referred to this genus have been found as far back as the Barremian stage of the Cedar Mountain Formation, dating to 125 million years ago.
There are 239 recorded fossil occurrences of Richardoestesia in the Paleobiology Database.
Some studies speculate that Richardoestesia had a piscivorous lifestyle based on its prevalence in marine environments.
If Richardoestesia was a dromaeosaurid, it would have been medium-sized, reaching 2 meters in length, 0.70 meters in height, and weighing 50 kilograms.
Because only teeth are known, the animal's relationships are obscure, but the teeth resemble those of Archaeopteryx, troodontids, or dromaeosaurids due to a strong lateral canal.

Relationships are obscure due to many plesiomorphies, leading to proposals to include it in various groups like ornithomimosaurians, tericinosaurids, oviraptorosaurs, alvarezsaurids, troodontids, but it is now most accepted to include it among dromaeosaurids.
The parent group of Richardoestesia is the family Dromaeosauridae.
Richardoestesia is classified within the class Reptilia.
Researchers consider Richardoestesia a morphogenus or form taxon because teeth attributed to it vary widely in age and location.
Richardoestesia lived during the Late Cretaceous Campanian stage, approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago, in what is now North America.
The genus Richardoestesia lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Maastrichtian, spanning from 154.8 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether the teeth of R. isosceles belong to Richardoestesia or to a crocodyliform, possibly a sebecosuchian, due to their shape.
Researchers doubt that all referred teeth belong to the same genus or species due to disparities in their location and age.
It is considered better to treat the genus as a morphotaxonomy rather than a single valid species.
